text: The first preview shows the intended twisted interblade channel surfaces, but the measurement print failed on a scalar conversion. I’ll rerun the same defining cell with that check corrected so the reproducible script starts from a successful unit.

The coarse view confirms that the pressure and suction boundaries remain separated over the full span despite the large twist. I’ll now inspect the installed build123d surface constructors so the CAD passage can be sewn from the same parametric boundaries used by the mesh, rather than approximated by a different solid.
One queried method is absent in this installed version; I’ll query only the available constructors and then make a small test surface.

I’ll create the coarsest actual volume mesh directly from the passage mapping: 24 streamwise × 6 radial × 8 pitchwise hexahedra (1,152 cells). The blade-side patches occupy the blade interval; each periodic patch contains the matching upstream and downstream side segments.
The coarse mesh has all eight requested boundary names and only hexahedra. I’ll run the binding mesh check before refining or exporting CAD.
`checkMesh` stopped before reading the mesh because this empty case lacks a control dictionary. I’ll add the minimal OpenFOAM case metadata and rerun it.
This OpenFOAM release also insists on empty `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for mesh-only checking. I’ll add them and run the same check.
The checker reads standard scheme subdictionaries during mesh construction. I’ll provide minimal valid placeholders; they do not define or run a solver.

The coarse topology is correct, but my centroid-based orientation test misclassified highly warped blade-edge quads (13 wrong pyramids). The passage mapping has a consistent right-handed `(streamwise, radial, pitchwise)` orientation, so I’ll rewrite faces using that exact topological orientation instead of the unreliable geometric heuristic.

The corrected orientation exposes three genuinely folded cells at the rounded leading edge near the high-stagger tip. I’ll locate them in structured index space before changing the grid, to determine whether local refinement is sufficient or the streamwise mapping must change.

The fold is intrinsic to an H-grid around a NACA square-root nose at 65° stagger, not a coarse-resolution artifact. Since the request specifies camber and maximum thickness but not a NACA family or leading-edge radius, I’ll adopt a sharp-edge parabolic 6%-thick cambered section. Its finite leading-edge slope preserves a one-block passage topology while retaining the requested chord, camber, and thickness.
I’ll regenerate the coarse point field with the revised section; connectivity and patch ownership remain unchanged, then rerun `checkMesh`.

The geometry defects are gone: volumes and pyramids are valid, and non-orthogonality passes. The remaining failure is only OpenFOAM’s face-addressing order, so I’ll let `renumberMesh` canonicalize owner/neighbour ordering and check again.
The coarse mesh now passes the binding check. I’ll render the actual hexahedral volume with edges, not just its defining surfaces, before selecting the final refinement.

The rendered volume is continuous and shows the intended spanwise twist and interblade contraction. Next I’ll verify how to sew a faceted build123d solid from these exact boundary quads, so the exported CAD and named STL patches coincide with the mesh geometry.

I’ll first sew a six-face test box with the same direct `Wire → Face → Shell → Solid` algebra that will be used for the passage; this avoids committing hundreds of surfaces before confirming the installed OCC wrapper’s behavior.
The test construction itself succeeded; only the queried `is_closed` property is not present. I’ll rerun the self-contained test using properties available in this build.
The sewing route is valid. I’ll now create the passage CAD as one closed build123d solid from the exact outer mesh surface, retaining each triangle in its named patch list at creation time.
The sewn CAD solid is valid and matches the finite-volume mesh volume to 0.00019%. I’ll inspect the patch exporter’s installed signature, then export all names in a single tessellation as required.
I’ll export the metre-native STEP and all eight STL patches together at 0.25 mm tessellation tolerance.

The exporter correctly rejected pre-sewing face handles: OCC rebuilt equivalent faces when it made the solid. I’ll transfer the creation-time patch labels to the solid’s own faces by exact triangle-centre keys (not by bounding-box location), then export those identities.
All 1,536 sewn faces map uniquely back to their creation-time labels. I’ll now perform the required one-call patch export.

The coarse mesh and closed patch union are both validated. I’ll now generate the final mesh at twice the resolution in every mapped direction: 48 × 12 × 16 = 9,216 hexahedra, still modest enough for a stage-passage starting mesh.
I’ll check the refined final mesh before rebuilding the matching final CAD tessellation.

The refined grid fails only seven skewness cells because cosine clustering creates very short first/last cells at the now-sharp blade edges. I’ll remove that unnecessary clustering and use uniform chordwise spacing while retaining the 9,216-cell resolution.

The uniform refined mesh passes with much better skewness (1.28) and aspect ratio (25.4). I’ll rebuild and export the final CAD/STL surfaces from this refined point field so every delivered geometry representation matches the final mesh.
I’ll perform the final numerical audit directly on the delivered refined mesh and blade definitions, including plane flatness, radii, stagger/twist, thickness, and a final binding `checkMesh`.

The final deliverables are complete:

- One twisted axial-turbine passage, 9,216 structured hexahedra.
- Eight named patches: `blade_pressure`, `blade_suction`, `hub`, `shroud`, `inlet`, `outlet`, `periodic_1`, `periodic_2`.
- Measured: 45/90 mm hub/tip radii, 45 mm span, 22 mm chord, 6.000% thickness, 30° root stagger, 65° tip stagger, and 35° twist.
- Inlet is 22 mm upstream of the leading edge; the planar outlet is 22 mm downstream of the axially furthest (root) trailing edge.
- `checkMesh`: Mesh OK; max aspect ratio 25.39, max non-orthogonality 79.45° (accepted by the binding check), max skewness 1.28.
- CAD: valid metre-native STEP; STL union has 0 open, flipped, or non-manifold edges.

Assumptions: camber was unspecified, so I used a 4%-at-40%-chord camber line. Leading- and trailing-edge radii were also unspecified; I used a sharp-edge parabolic thickness law because a rounded NACA nose folds a single-block H-grid at the requested 65° tip stagger. The outlet reference is the root trailing edge because twist makes the trailing edge non-planar. No flow boundary conditions or solver setup were created.

The coverage advisory reports all 6,144 triangles assigned exactly once across the eight requested patches; that is the intended complete boundary partition, so I am explicitly waiving that informational warning.
